analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety rules, penalties, and whistleblower protections for coal and other miners.
analysis.headline: The mine safety bill drew three Senate Democrats as supporters, but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal mine safety law to give miners stronger legal protection when they report unsafe conditions, make it easier to shut down dangerous mines, raise fines and criminal penalties for operators who knowingly violate safety rules, and require new safety equipment and training in underground coal mines. It would also extend federal workplace safety rules to government employees for the first time. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners, especially the roughly tens of thousands working underground in coal mines, along with their families. Miners would get independent investigations of major accidents, protection from being fired for reporting hazards, guaranteed pay when a mine is closed by a safety order, refresher training that includes their legal rights, a toll-free hotline for reporting dangers, and lower dust levels and monitoring systems to reduce explosion and black lung risks. All government employees would gain workplace safety coverage under the OSH Act for the first time.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates an independent panel, chaired by a federal mine safety research official, to investigate any mining accident involving three or more deaths, with subpoena power and confidential interviews that mine operators cannot monitor [S2][S3].

It strengthens protection from retaliation: miners who report hazards, injuries, or refuse unsafe work could not be fired or disciplined, could be quickly reinstated, and could not be forced to waive these rights through arbitration agreements [S2][S3].

It raises the stakes for operators: knowingly violating a safety standard becomes a federal crime with up to a $250,000 fine and a year in prison, up to $1 million and five years for repeat offenders, and up to $2 million and ten years for violations that recklessly expose miners to death or serious injury; officers and directors who order violations would be personally liable [S2][S3].

It requires underground coal mines to brief miners on hazardous conditions before each shift, install atmospheric monitoring systems for methane and carbon monoxide, raise rock dusting requirements from 65 to 80 percent to prevent coal dust explosions, and give miners at least nine hours of annual refresher training [S2][S3].

It guarantees pay for miners idled when a mine or work area is closed by a safety order, and prohibits operators of mines with repeated serious violations from firing hourly miners without cause [S3].
It extends coverage of the Occupational Safety and Health Act to government employees, who are currently excluded from federal workplace safety law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators bear the cost: higher civil fines including doubled penalties for mines with a pattern of violations, personal criminal liability for officers and directors, the cost of atmospheric monitoring systems and safety equipment, expanded training and recordkeeping, and the lost production that comes with more frequent shutdowns of unsafe mines. State and local governments would take on the cost of complying with the newly extended OSH Act for their employees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and mining company executives

drawbacks.text: Compliance would cost money at a time when coal companies were already under financial strain, and the bill itself acknowledges concerns about delays by ordering a government study on how quickly the Mine Safety and Health Administration approves underground mine plans [S3].

The bill gives the Secretary of Labor broad new authority to revoke approved mine plans and order mines emptied, and limits courts' ability to second-guess those decisions, which operators would argue concentrates significant power in one agency [S3].
Expanding OSH Act coverage to all government employees imposes new inspection, recordkeeping, and abatement costs on state, county, and city governments [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The human stakes are large: mine disasters kill multiple miners at once, and many of the bill's provisions respond directly to failures documented in past accidents, such as operators notifying miners in advance of inspections, disabling safety devices, and firing miners who raise concerns. The costs fall on a specific industry whose balance sheets were already stressed, and some provisions (like doubled penalties and broad agency shutdown authority) could be drawn more narrowly. On balance, the bill trades real compliance and enforcement costs for safety rules that mainly protect workers' lives and health.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2017 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, it sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Casey of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on April 5, 2017, joined by Sens. Joe Manchin and Sherrod Brown; both signed on as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that referral was the bill's final action of record [S5].
The committee never took the bill up, and no Senate version advanced in the 115th Congress; the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off: they avoided the higher fines, personal criminal exposure for executives, mandated monitoring equipment, and expanded shutdown authority the bill would have imposed. Miners gained no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal mine operators, who avoided new penalties and costs

for.name: Sen. Bob Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: United Mine Workers of America
for.what_they_did: Long advocated for the mine safety reforms in this bill, which closely track the union's legislative agenda after past mine disasters.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never received a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate supporters were Democrats, there were no Republican cosponsors, and the bill stalled in a Republican-chaired committee without ever reaching the floor.

industries.note: The bill raises civil fines (up to $220,000 for specific violations and doubled penalties for chronic violators), makes knowingly violating safety standards a felony with up to five years in prison, and holds officers and directors personally liable. Its interest in avoiding penalties and shutdowns runs directly against miners' interest in safe conditions.

industries.industry: Mining safety equipment and monitoring technology makers
industries.note: Mandated atmospheric monitoring systems, direct-reading coal dust explosibility monitors, and electronic recordkeeping requirements would create demand for safety equipment. More of that equipment means earlier warning of methane and carbon monoxide buildup for miners.
Extending OSH Act coverage to government employees means new compliance and abatement costs for public employers, while their workers gain federal workplace safety protections they currently lack.

The bill brings independent contractors within the definition of 'operator,' making them responsible for reporting injuries and liable under the same standards, while their workers gain the same protections as miners.
